lines.text: I can hold my breath longer than Ravi.
That cloud is a dog. That one is also a dog.
I am not tired. My legs are tired.
Watch me. Watch me. Nobody is watching.
Meera says crabs can't feel it. She lies.
Wind's turning. I can smell the green in it.
My knee has a scab shaped like a boot.
Two more knots and then I'm done forever.
Tan ate the last of the salt fish. Tan did.
I'm allowed to. Mostly.
Counting to a hundred. Don't talk.
If you spin fast the sky spins slower.
Bet I can throw it further than that.
Nobody knows where my other sandal went. Nobody.
Don't tell. I mean it. Don't tell.
Kalyani is it. Kalyani is always it.
I'm hungry. I was hungry before as well.
The gulls know my name. They shout it.
Sharpening this stick. It's for nothing.
It's warm in the back. That's where I sit.
Not allowed past the third lamp.
The seed jars are cold. I lick them.
My voice comes back at me down there.
There are books. I can read four words.
The bats go out at the same time every night.
My fingers went white. Look at them.
It's cold. It's always cold. I'm mentioning it.
We only wash on the warm days.
The fire is mine to watch. I'm watching it.
Ice on the bucket again this morning.
Nothing grows here except the grey moss stuff.
You can see the weather coming before it arrives.
Half these houses have nobody. I go in them.
This shell has a hole. That makes it a whistle.
That roof has a bird living in it now.
The empty house makes a noise when it's windy.
My mother says decide. My father says soon.
Nobody stops me here. There's nobody to stop me.
I know which doors still shut. Three.
They make me say the numbers back. Every day.
Chalk on my hands again.
The terrace wall fell down. Not me that time.
The goats eat better than we do.
It has to be neat or it doesn't count.
Beans. Beans. Beans. Beans.
Up here the wind gets inside your ears.
Bailing. Bailing. Bailing. Bailing.
The plank by our door sings when you jump.
I sleep over the water. I hear it all night.
Ravi fell off the walkway again. On purpose.
Rope's gone furry. That means change it.
Caught a needlefish. It bit me. Worth it.
Our house wobbles when Tan runs. Good wobble.
Step on the grey plank, not the pale one.
The bucket's cracked. I put my thumb over it.
I can do a flip. A proper one, off the top, all the way over. I'm not doing it now though.
Ravi says if you eat the eyes you can see in the dark. I've eaten four. Nothing yet.
There's a bird that comes when it's going to rain. Grey, cross-looking, one leg shorter than the other. Her name is Betta. I named her, so it is.
I'm not scared of the big crabs. I am careful of them. That is a different thing and my mother agrees with me.
We're not allowed to play the shouting game near the mending. So we play it just far enough off that it doesn't count as near.
Meera says her hair grew long in one night. It didn't. I saw it the day before and it was exactly the same hair.
My job is stones. I pick the stones out of the beans. It is the worst job there is and I am extremely good at it.
Tan can whistle through his teeth and I can't. I have been practising eleven days. It comes out as breath.
If you hold still long enough a lizard will walk on you. I got one up to my elbow before I laughed and ruined it.
It never rains inside and the back part is never cold. When it's blowing out there you can hear it at the mouth and it can't get in. Best place there is.
My voice goes down the long bit and comes back different. Deeper. Like somebody much bigger is agreeing with me.
There are jars along the wall taller than me, full of seeds, and I'm not to touch them. So I count them instead. Forty-one. I have counted it wrong before.
In the morning the bucket has a lid of ice on it and you can lift the whole lid off in one piece. That is my job. Nobody else is allowed.
I keep the fire from dark until food. Small ones first, then the big one at the end. It has not gone out on me. Not once.
We eat the same thing at the same time every day. Once there was honey, and I can tell you exactly where I was sitting.
There are seven empty houses and I have been inside six. The last one has a wasp thing in the roof and I am waiting for winter.
We keep saying we're going. My mother says it in the morning. Then at night she goes out and plants something.
The house with no roof is the best house. The rain comes straight in and you can stand in it and nobody says get out of the rain.
They make us say the year list. Every name, in order, back and back. Get one wrong and you start again from the front. Meera never gets one wrong and it makes me want to bite her.
I built a wall of my own. It's small. It fell over twice and then it stayed up, and now it holds four beans in.
The goats know their own names and I do not know all of theirs. That is embarrassing for me and I am working on it.
You write the numbers in the book with the good ink, and if you blot it you go and sit outside. I have sat outside twice.
Our whole house moves a bit. It isn't broken, it's meant to. When the wind is up my bed swings and I pretend it's a fight I'm winning.
You dive off the corner post, not the middle. The middle has the anchor rope under it and the rope takes your skin off. Everybody knows that. Ravi didn't.
I bail before food and after food. Two buckets each time. My arms are getting big. Feel them. No, properly.
There's a fish that lives under our floor. Fat, striped, sulky. My father says catch it. I say she lives there, so no.
The old ones say it was different. They say lots of things.
My grandmother's house is a fish house now.
When I'm big the water will be at my chin. Fine.
I've never seen it go down. Not once.
I swim better than I walk. Ask anyone.
Meera says there were roads down there. Roads. Ha.
One day this hill will be an island. Great.
You can't drown if you're good at it.
I have a comb the water gave back. Six teeth.
My mother moved when she was little. I haven't moved yet.
More of my family is under than up here.
I'm living on a raft when I'm big. Decided.
The sea took our step. Just the one step so far.
Nobody remembers dry. Not even the very old ones.
The water comes up a hand a year. My hand's small.
There's a roof out there you can stand on.
The water isn't going anywhere. It lives here.
The dead are in here. They don't mind me.
The seeds are for when. Nobody says when.
People have slept in here forever. Forever forever.
This cave has never once been wet.
There's a jar with my great-great-someone in it.
The books talk about places that aren't there.
The oldest name on the wall is a lady.
The lower villages are specks. Moving specks.
You can't hear the sea from up here at all.
The old ones came up carrying doors. Doors!
We're the highest. That's a fact and I'm saying it.
Three drowned roofs on a clear day. I count them.
It takes two days to walk down to the water.
That house drank. Nobody goes in it now.
We moved once. We'll move again. Everyone says so.
Salt got in the well. It tastes like the beach.
The lane ends in water. Good for jumping.
They took the door with them. Just the door.
The tide comes into the kitchen twice a moon.
There's a boat in the hedge. Been there ages.
Two families left this year. I got their chickens.
The bottom of our street is a beach now.
We moved up in my mother's time. Before me.
They write down where the water got to. In a book.
Our terraces are wonky. Everybody says so. Nobody fixes them.
Everybody here came from somewhere lower down.
We're safe up here. They keep saying it like that.
A mark on the rock for every year. I counted wrong.
The water people call us runners. I like running.
That was a street. Now it's where I fish.
My father's room is down there. Two doors along.
The old ladder goes down into the green.
We put the floor up higher last winter.
You can see the roof tiles when it's still.
The stilts got longer twice since I was born.
Grandad's window has a fish family in it.
My uncle dives with a stone to go faster.
We bail every morning. It's boring, not sad.
My grandmother's kitchen is under the water. I've been in it. There's a shelf and the shelf still has a pot on it, sideways, and it stays like that.
People from up the hill come down and look at the water and go quiet. It's just the water. It's been doing that the whole time. I don't know what they're looking for.
I'm going to be the best swimmer of anyone ever. That's easy. The ones before me had all that ground to walk about on, so they got no practice.
When I'm old the water will be up at the tall tree. I worked it out on my fingers. So I'll live above the tall tree. I've thought about it, it's fine.
Everything good is at the bottom. Cups and combs and doors. That's where the old people kept their things, at the bottom, and that is why it's all under now.
You can tell how old a wall is by how wet it is. The wettest wall is the oldest wall. I worked that out myself and nobody has said no yet.
My father says don't go past the second post. So I go to the second post and put my hand on it and look, and that isn't past.
There's a bell out there somewhere and the sea has got it. Nobody agrees where. I say everybody should shut up at the same time and listen, and nobody will do it.
The dead are all in the back in the jars, and I'm meant to be quiet in there, but I sing, because the sound goes round and round and they have heard worse.
This cave has never been wet. Not one time, not in anybody's anybody's time. So it is the winning place. And it's still just a cave.
There are seeds in here for growing things that don't grow here any more. I asked when we're planting them. Nobody said a number.
From up here the sea is just a shine along the bottom of everything. You can't see it doing anything. It is, though. Very slowly, which is the sneaky way.
The first ones who came up here carried doors on their backs. Actual doors. I don't know what they were going to put them in, but they weren't leaving them behind.
Nobody will ever have to move from here, my grandfather says. Then he goes out and looks down at the water and comes back in. Every day. Same time.
I walked down to the water once with my brother. Two days there. The bottom is warm and loud and crowded and everything smells of something. I want to live there.
That house drank last winter. It took some in and then it sat down. It had been empty for ages before that, but I still say sorry when I go past.
We're moving. We have been moving for two years. The cart is packed and the goat is ready and my mother keeps finding one more thing that has to be done first.
Half our garden went salty. The salty half goes grey and crunchy and you can snap a whole plant with your foot. That's the only good part of it.
Nobody fixes anything here any more. If a shutter goes, it goes. My father says there's no sense putting a good hinge on a house you're leaving. Then he oils the hinge.
My aunt's tree is standing in the sea up past its knees and it still has leaves on. She's dead and the tree isn't. I said that out loud and got told off.
We came up in my mother's mother's time, before anybody I know. So I have never had to go anywhere. I would quite like to have to.
There's a book with where the water got to written in it, every year, going back and back and back. I'm allowed to turn the pages if my hands are dry.
They cut this hill into steps because there's a place far off cut into steps and that place stayed up. Ours keep falling down. So either we're doing it wrong or that place is lying.
The ones down on the water call us runners and they laugh when they say it. My uncle laughs back. Then he's quiet for a bit after.
That was a street down there. My mother walked on it. Now I swim over it, and swimming is better than walking, so I don't know what she's sad about.
You can see our old door on a still day. Green, with the bar across. I go down and touch it every summer. It's a rule I made.
We put the floor higher last winter. Everything came out, then the boards went up on the blocks, then everything went back in. Four days. I carried the small things.
There's a whole roof under our boat and in summer the fish sit on it like it's theirs. Which it is now, I suppose. I'd let them.
The hill people won't sleep over water. They say it's mad. I say sleeping on a hill is mad, because nothing moves at all, so how do you get off to sleep?
I can hold my breath for ages. Ages.
Watch me. Watch. Watch me do it.
Tan says the eels are people. They're not.
I'm hungry. I'm very hungry.
Tan cried at a fish. A small one.
I found a hinge. It's mine now.
That roof was Gran's. The mossy one.
Nobody swims down there except me.
That's not a rock. That's a step.
Salt makes my hair go stiff.
Great-gran is in the third room along.
Don't shake the seed jars.
No running past the dead. That's the rule.
The books are for later. Later is boring.
I know which jar is beans.
It smells like dust and old rope.
Bones are just bones. I've touched one.
Some names are just scratches now.
The deep room is colder. That's where they go.
That flat water was a square. Papa says.
My hands are cold. Always cold.
You can see the whole water from here.
Nothing grows up here. Only rocks.
Papa says it's warm down there. So go.
The wind takes the washing every single time.
We burn dung. It stinks.
Nobody goes down from here. Too far.
I came up in a basket. Don't remember it.
Nobody lives in the blue house. So it's ours.
The lane goes into the water and stops.
We're moving again. Third time for me.
The pig went uphill without us. Traitor.
Four houses left. One is ours.
Mama counts the pots every single night.
Everything we own fits in six baskets.
The bell house is empty. We play in it.
Half the doors are gone. People took them.
They write the water down. Every week. Boring.
The ink went brown on the old pages.
Our old road is in the book. I looked.
They keep the old street names. For nothing.
The list of drowned lanes is very long.
We eat goat. I want fish.
Nobody up here can swim. Nobody.
The measuring stick has notches all the way up.
The old maps are wrong now. That's funny.
Our raft is named Perla. Perla was Mama's sister.
I can touch the green door. Ravi can't.
Our house has a house under it.
Bail faster. I'm winning.
I sleep on top of somebody's kitchen.
Ravi's ladder ends at his grandad's roof.
Meera dropped a spoon down the stairs. Years ago.
The good handhold is the window with bars.
Two knocks means the water's over the boards.
I can get to the bottom of the well house in one breath. Ravi gets halfway and comes up saying he swallowed something. He always swallows something.
My aunt's window is the round one with the bars. Mama says don't go in. I go to the bars and look and then I come back up, so that is not going in.
Everyone gets sad about the old town. I have only ever seen it wet. It is better wet. There are fish in the doorways and you can swim through a window like a bird.
Tan is scared of the deep bit. I told him the deep bit is just a road. He said roads don't have eels in. They do now.
I know four names of dead people and one of them is a boat.
Meera says her grandmother's chair is still down there facing the same way it always faced. I dived and it isn't a chair. I didn't tell her.
Grown-ups say the word before like it's a place you could walk to. Before, before, before. I say it too but I don't know where it is.
I'm hungry. That's it. That's the thing I wanted to say.
My name was somebody else's first and she is dead. Everybody says I have her chin. So I have got a dead lady's chin, which is not my fault.
The best thing about a drowned house is you go in through the roof. No door. You just fall in very slowly and land on the ceiling from the wrong side.
There's a bell down there somewhere. I've never heard it ring. But if you go all the way down and hold still and stop your ears wobbling, you nearly do.
Great-gran is in the third room in a niche with her name scratched over the top. We take her a bit of bread on her day. She doesn't eat it. Somebody eats it.
The jars have seeds in from before anybody. If you shake one you get shouted at by four adults at the same time, which I know because I did it.
The names go all the way round the room and then start again in a row above, and then again above that. Three rows. They keep having to start higher.
From the flat rock you can count roofs down in the water. Today there were nine. Some days it's six, because the light is wrong, not because the roofs went anywhere.

Papa carried me up here in a basket when I was small. He tells it like it was the hardest thing anyone ever did. I don't remember it, so as far as I'm concerned I have always been up here and he can stop.
It's cold, there's no fish, and the goat hates everybody. But from our door you can see the whole water at once. Down there they can only see the bit they're standing in.
Mama says everyone carries something when we go. I said I'll carry the cat. Now I have to carry the cat, and the cat has opinions, so that was a mistake.
The blue house has nobody in it so we made it ours. There's a mark on the doorframe where somebody measured a kid. The kid got taller than me and then went away.
People take the doors with them when they leave. Just the doors. So there are houses standing there with holes where the doors were and you can walk straight in and nobody minds.
Everyone here is going and nobody has gone. They talk about it at every single meal. I said just go then, and got sent outside, and outside was better anyway.

They write the water down in a book every week. One line, one number. It is the most boring book there is. But our old road is in it, and the road isn't anywhere now, so the book has more road than the world does.
I have never touched the sea. I've looked at it every day of my whole life and never once touched it. When I say that to the raft kids they laugh until they fall over.
Grandpa is on page eleven. Just his name, the year, and a little sum at the end. That's all a person gets in there. He was much bigger than a line.
Our raft is Perla. Perla was Mama's sister and she went under with a boat, and now she is a raft, which is better than being nothing. I'm not allowed to say that at supper.
Under our floorboards there's a chimney. On a still day when the water goes clear you can see right down it. Nothing ever comes out. I've watched for ages.
The green door still has its handle on. I go down and hold the handle and turn it and it turns, every time, and then my chest starts going and I have to come up.
Bailing is boring but I'm the fastest at it, and being fastest at a boring thing is still being fastest.
The water stops at the pointy ones. Everyone knows.
There's a hole in the Wall. Somebody's finding it.
The lions drank there. Enormous lions.
It's a cup. A big cup for rain.
Nobody built Petra. They took rock away.
You read the corners. That's how the stone works.
The white one is a box for one dead lady.
Even Ravi doesn't argue about the white one.
Build steps and you live. That's it.
Seven. I counted on fingers. Seven.
They knew it was coming. They built it in stone.
Chicken Itza. That is really its name.
The Wall is a dam. It broke ages ago.
Petra is from before. So there was a before.
Meera says eight wonders. Meera can't count.
The stone said this winter. The stone lied.
Water can't get in the cup. Already full.
Ask three people. Get four wonders.
The drawing of the white tomb is the good one.
The oldest book never mentions water. Weird.
Petra is a cave. A fancy one.
Nobody gets a tomb like that now. Nobody.
The book says the Wall held. Book's old.
Down here it's dry. Like Petra. Probably.
The wall names go back further than the wonders.
Ravi says the seeds came from a wonder. No.
The Wall is that way. Papa points wrong every time.
We're higher than the steps place. So we win.
You can see three wonders from the ridge. Two.
The Wall goes on forever. I've seen the end.
Pilgrims want salt. Always salt.
The builders lived up high. Obviously.
The white tomb is south. Or north. South.
Nobody here has walked to the Wall. Cowards.
Pilgrims sleep in the empty houses. Free beds.
Everyone quotes the stone. Nobody has seen it.
Half of us are going to the steps place. Half.
A man asked about the breach. We said which breach.
The wonder people never had to move. Lucky.
Their rope was better than our rope. Obviously.
Our terraces slump every spring. Theirs never do.
Everything gets written down. Even the arguing.
They measured the pointy one off a drawing. Ha.
Page one is the Wall. Page two is the hole.
Two books, two answers. Both ours.
The record man draws lions with square feet.
I turn the pages. Not the brown ones.
Somebody crossed out a whole year. Rude.
Papa's cousin went to walk the Wall. Still walking.
Our stilts are like the steps place. Sort of.
We're not moving. The wonders didn't move.
Hill people copy the steps. We copy nothing.
Papa laughed at the pointy ones. Then stopped.
The counting stone never mentions our house.
I'd rather live in the cup. It's round.
The pointy ones are markers. People built them long ago because they knew, and they put the top exactly where the water stops. So when it gets to the top it stops. That's what a marker is for.
There's a hole in the Wall. That's why all this happened. When somebody finds the hole and plugs it, the water goes back down and everyone goes home and I get my own room.
The round one is a cup. It held the drinking water for everybody, and the lions drank there too, down at the low end, because a lion would empty your bucket in one go.

Nobody built Petra. They took rock away instead of piling it up, which is backwards. And you cannot carve a rock underwater, so it was before the water, so there was a before. Ravi says there wasn't. Ravi is an idiot.
The counting stone tells you the water. You read the corners and it gives you a year. Old Neru says it says nothing, but Old Neru can't read the corners, he just looks at them.
The white one is a tomb for one person. One. A whole building for one dead lady. Everybody agrees about it, and everybody never agrees about anything, so it must be true.
There are seven big things and they are all still standing, and every little thing is under. So little things drown and big things don't. I worked that out by myself.
The steps place is how you're meant to build. Flat bit, wall, flat bit, wall, all the way up a mountain. If we'd built like that we'd be fine. We built like idiots.
Meera says the wonders were made by giants. They were not. They were made by people who knew, which is worse, because that means somebody knew and went and built a wall instead of telling anyone.
The ones who made the pointy ones knew what was coming. So somewhere there is a list of it, all written out in order. I want the list. Nobody has got the list.
I'm going to make a wonder. It will have steps, and a hole for the water to go in, and my name cut into the front, and it will still be standing when every single other thing is under.
People argue about all of them except the white tomb. You say the white tomb and everybody goes quiet and nods, even the two who won't share a fire.
The wonders don't leak. That's the whole thing about them. Our roof is four years old and it leaks in two places, and theirs is a thousand years old and it doesn't.
The Wall held it all back once, like a bowl holds soup. Then it cracked. I've never seen a crack that big, but it's a very long wall and people give up in the middle.
There's a book down here with all seven drawn in it and two pages torn out, so there might have been nine. Nobody will say which two are missing. I think they don't know either.

Somebody scratched a little pointy one on the wall by the seed room, low down, where a kid would reach. It's older than my grandmother's grandmother. So a kid did that ages ago and then died, and the scratch is still going.
Up here is like the steps place. Flat bits and walls, only colder and worse. Build like that and you live, they say, usually while somebody's toes are going black.
The pilgrims come over the pass in spring in terrible boots, off to walk the Wall. They ask which way and we point and they go. None of them has ever come back over the pass the other way.

Pilgrims came through wanting bread and we gave them some. They're walking the whole Wall looking for the break in it. They've been walking six years. I asked if they'd found it yet and one of them looked at me for a long time.
The counting stone told a family up the coast to move, so they moved, and their house is fine. Ours is fine as well and we never moved. Nobody talks about that bit.
We could go and live at the steps place. It has flat bits all the way up and nothing there has ever drowned. Mama says it isn't that simple. Nothing is ever that simple in this house.
We copy the steps place with our terraces, and ours slump every spring, and theirs are still perfectly straight after forever. So we're doing some bit of it wrong and nobody will say which bit.
The book has a drawing of the pointy ones with the water line marked along the side. Different people marked different lines. There are four lines on it now. They can't all be the right one.
The record man wrote down that the counting stone predicts nothing. Then underneath, in small letters, he wrote down what it predicted anyway. Just in case, I think.
On a clear evening from our roof there's a bump on the edge of the water, right at the end. Mama says it's a cloud. It is not a cloud. Clouds move and that has never moved once.
When they plug the Wall the water goes down and our house will be standing up in the air on its legs like a bird. Then we'll need stairs. Proper stairs, to the ground.

Ravi says a lion swims past the poles at night. Lions drank at the round place and the round place is days away, so it would have to be a very good swimmer. I still don't go out past the poles at night.
I can write my name. Twice.
My S goes backwards on purpose.
Nobody ever watches the good jump.
Grown ups only talk about up.
I'm not learning the long words.
Everyone stops talking when I walk in.
Ask me a letter. Ask me one.
I'm hungry and nobody is doing anything.
Reading is guessing but slower.
They argued about a ladder all night.
Books smell like feet.
I know the alphabet up to M.
Everything good is under something.
I drew our house. The next one.
Grown ups cry facing away.
When I'm big I'll live higher than everyone.
Watch this bit. You missed it.
My name is four letters. Ravi's is too.
Tan says the water gets tired eventually.
Meera bit the teacher. It was brilliant.
They said not to tell me yet.
I'm going to be the one who stays.
The seed jars. I'm not allowed.
Put your hand on the wall. Cold.
Great-aunt Sura is in the third alcove.
Shout in here and it shouts back.
The book room is the dry room.
I know which jar is the wheat.
Same weather in here. Always.
I do my letters in the dust.
The dead get the driest shelf.
My fingers went white again. Look.
Beans. Beans forever.
You can see the whole sea from our door.
The goat is warmer than my bed.
Highest house in the world. Ours.
The wind takes your paper if you write outside.
Snow tastes like nothing. I checked.
Gran sits closest to the fire. Always.
Up here the sea is just a floor.
Four houses left. I counted twice.
The empty ones are the best ones.
The bell house has no bell now.
Nobody lives behind the blue door.
I'm allowed in any house now.
They took the hinges. Left the beds.
My friend moved up. She got taller.
Half this street is only doorways.
The packing baskets are out again.
I have to copy the list again. Neatly.
They write everything down here. Even sneezes.
My handwriting is the best. Ask anyone.
Mum says we're not smug. We're smug.
Our terrace wall fell down again.
The list has my name on it. Third.
Numbers, numbers, then dinner.
The book room smells of onions.
I ring the bell at the measuring post.
We build like the stone city. Badly.
I bail with the little bucket. It counts.
Floor's wetter than yesterday. Fine.
Dad says one more year on the stilts.
My frog lives here so I'm not moving.
The ladder got a new rung today.
Books on the high shelf again.
I sleep in the dry corner now.
The teacher won't come out to the raft.
I can walk the pontoon backwards.
Our front step is a diving step.
They keep asking each other whether it's worth teaching us letters. I'm sat right there. I can hear them. So now I'm learning out of spite and I'm going to be extremely good at it.
Everyone says the water stops when it reaches the markers. Then they say maybe. I don't mind which, I just want to be told once and have it stay told.
When I'm grown I'll have a house with three floors and I'll use the top one for nothing at all. Just an empty room. That's what being grown is.
Grown ups have a face for when I ask how long. It's the same face on all of them, every time. They must go somewhere and practise it together.
I know the letters up to M and after that it goes silly. Two of them make the same noise. Whoever did it should have stopped while it was going well.
Mum says learn to read so you can tell them. Tell who. She says the ones after us. There's no after, there's just us and then more of us, which is the same thing.
I'm the best swimmer of anyone my size, which is useful, and reading isn't. I'm doing both anyway because otherwise Gran does the wobbly voice.
The old ones talk about going up like it's an enormous decision. We go up all the time. We went up before I was born and I turned out fine.
