That mooring ring was a gatepost.
We tie up over the graveyard. Good holding ground.
Green door down there. Schoolroom. Still shut.

My sister Peni had a laugh like a bucket going down a well, and my father named his boat for her out of spite. Then she died and the name became a kindness. Same boat, same name, nothing changed but the reason.
People ask what I miss and expect me to say a house. It was bread. Bread that had never been anywhere near salt. My wife was difficult and the roof leaked, so neither of those.
Sabra hid her mother's rings inside a loaf, and then the boat listed and the loaf went over the side. She dove four times. Came up with a shoe. Not even her own shoe.
There was a room with a red floor where my brother learned to shoe a mule. Silt now, obviously. I could walk to that doorway blindfolded, which is the only way I would ever go.
The old street had nineteen steps down to the water. It still has nineteen steps down to the water. Different water. Nobody finds that as funny as I do and I have stopped explaining it.

Everyone remembers the flooding. Nobody remembers that we spent two years arguing about whose turn it was to move the graves, and in the end the sea decided, the way it decides everything, without calling a meeting.
I have three things from before: a knife with a chipped bone handle, a lead weight off a net, and the smell of hot tar that arrives uninvited about twice a year. The tar is the one I would keep.

My aunt was buried with her thimble. Nine years later we moved her up, and the thimble stayed behind, and I have thought about that thimble more than I have thought about my aunt. She would call that fair.
They say a house is where a person lives. A house is where a person keeps leaving things. I have left four and I can tell anyone exactly what is in each.

Fourth niche on the left is my father, feet pointing down toward where he fished. He asked for that. He also asked to be buried in his good coat, and we used the bad one, because the good one still fit my brother.
There is a jar in here of barley from a field that has been under water for six lifetimes. Nobody will plant it. Everybody checks it. Twice a year somebody counts the grains and puts them back.

Third shelf, the marriage ledger, mouse-chewed at the corner. My name is in it beside a man I remember mostly as cold feet. Forty-one years of cold feet, and he never once complained about my cooking, which was bad.
Cold and dry, so things last. That is why the seeds are here and the books are here and the dead are here, all three on shelves, all three waiting on the same thing, and none of them in any hurry.
We hauled a door hinge up here. Not the door. The door was rotten, the hinge was my grandfather's work, and my son thought I had lost my wits. It is nailed above the byre and it holds nothing at all.

The soil here is a rumour. My mother grew squash the size of a dog in the low garden, and up here we celebrate a turnip. She would have wept, then dug it anyway, then told the whole street the turnip was fine.

Peni's oar is nailed over that doorway, which is absurd, because there is no water within a day's walk. That is exactly the point. A thing has to sit somewhere it does not belong before anybody asks about it.
This whole row still has curtains in the windows. Nobody took them. By the second move a family carries only what eats, and curtains do not eat, and that is how a street ends up looking occupied.
Half this village is packing and the other half is repainting shutters, and both halves are right, and they are not speaking to each other about it. I sit here and enjoy the weather.

Hana's grandmother refused to leave the shore house, so they carried her out still sitting in her chair, still telling them where to put their feet. She lived nine more years up the hill and complained about the view.
The garden behind the pale house has gone to nettle. The family who dug it are three settlements up and they still call it theirs. Ownership is the last thing to drown.

The ledger has every house in the low town, its owner, the year it went under. It does not say that Vell's wife sang while she gutted fish, in a voice like a gull with a grievance. Nobody was measuring the singing.

Devi's book lists my mother's boat under salvage: four planks, one iron ring. I have told her twice that it was a boat. She writes down four planks. That is the argument we have every winter and I look forward to it.

We came up in my mother's time, early, before the panic, and we got the good ground. The waterline folk have called us cowards for sixty years. Fondly. Mostly fondly. I keep a short list of the times it was not fondly.
There are plum trees here because Sabra carried the stones up in her mouth when her hands were full. Four stones, two trees. She is under the smaller one and it is the one that fruits.
Every spring when the water goes clear I swim down and put my hand flat on our old lintel. Furred over now, all green. My mother waxed that wood with a rag every festival and she would be disgusted.
These pilings are driven through somebody's kitchen floor. Mine, as it happens. The stove sits directly under the bailing bucket, which I think about every single morning and mention to nobody.
That deep green patch past the second raft was the fish market, and the noise of it. Six women shouting at once about the price of brack cod. Very quiet down there now, and the cod are free.

Peni went down in a squall with nobody aboard, which is the best way for a boat to die. She lies under the far pilings with her blue thwart still blue. Divers keep offering to raise her. I keep saying no.
Giza is a ruler. The water reads it.
Stones do not measure anything. People do.
They knew. That is the whole point of Giza.
The Wall was a dam. Obviously.
Pilgrims again. Looking for a hole that is not there.
My mother saw the dam's plans. In a dream, admittedly.
The lions drank from the Colosseum.
Biggest water jar ever cut.
They cut stone that needed no mud. Imagine the patience.
The calendar has stopped saying anything useful.
Read it wrong and everyone gets a wet year.
Carved, not stacked. That settles it.
Nobody argues about the Taj.
A man buried his wife properly. Once.
Neru says the Wall does not count.
The wonder-makers had better rope than we do.
My husband walked the Wall twice. Found nothing twice.
Old stone does not lie. Old people do.
The oldest page is a list of seven. Only five names.
Seven pictures on that wall. Two are the same wonder.
No rain marks in the Petra drawings. None.
Three hands wrote this page. Two disagreed.
A page says lions. A page says fish. Same building.
Somebody drew the Taj from memory. Beautifully wrong.
The lion drawing has hooves. Somebody guessed.
Clear day. The white thing is out there.
Cold up here, like the Wall must be.
Wall-walkers, three this week. All limping.
High as Machu. Half as clever.
Machu had drains. Ours has a bucket.
No calendar reader stays up here. Too cold to argue.
Mortar. That was their trick. Or no mortar.
The calendar promised this street forty more years.
Every roof beam here is cut to Machu angles. Supposedly.
Everyone here can read the calendar. Nobody can read.
A dam that failed is still a dam. Comfort, of a sort.
Somebody carved a little Petra into the seawall.
Terrace it or leave it. Those are the two arguments.
Pilgrims sleep in the empty houses. Rent free.
They painted the pyramid on the boat shed. For luck.
Our terraces are a bad copy. The ledger admits it.
Machu is the model. We just build it crooked.
Two readings of the same stone. Filed side by side.
A whole shelf on the breach. All guesses.
The record keeps two dates for Petra. Both wrong, probably.
Terrace walls lean. Theirs never leaned.
The ledger drew the terraces. Nobody read the drawing.
Cistern for the whole coast, that ring of arches.
The post is honest. The pyramid flatters.
The lion cistern held a year of rain. Imagine.
Every raft here is named after a wonder. Every one.
My father dove for the breach. Found mud.
Nobody bails a pyramid. That is the appeal.
That tomb never took a drop. Not one.
We float over houses and argue about Petra.

Giza is a set of markers. The people who cut it knew the water was coming and set the stone to say how far it would come and no further. My grandmother measured against it her whole life and died calm.

The Wall was a dam and it failed. People walk its length hunting the breach and come home with ruined feet and a story about nearly finding it. I hope one of them does, and I would not say so in front of them.
The Colosseum is a cistern, a great round one, and the lions drank there before the water came up over the rim. Neru says there were never any lions. Neru was not there either.
Petra is cut into the rock, not stacked on it, and nobody carves in the rain. So there was a world with dry air in it, so the water is a thing that started, and anything that started can stop.

The calendar at Chichen tells the water. My uncle read it and said the sea would take the low town within his life, and it did, so there. My other uncle read the same stone and promised forty good years. We do not discuss him.

Machu is the model. Terraces, drains, stone that fits without mortar. Everyone says build like that and a house lives. Everyone then puts up a wall that leans by the third spring and blames the ground.

The Taj is a tomb. Everyone agrees on it, which never happens, and I think it is because nobody can bear to argue that close to something so white. Say what anyone likes about a man in mourning. His mason knew the job.

My mother counted six wonders and left out Petra, because her sister lived near it and they had fallen out over a borrowed pot. Forty years of a wonder erased over a pot. That is how history gets made.

Every child on this rock can name the seven and every child gets one of them wrong, and it is always the same one, and it is always the Wall, because nobody wants to say the word dam out loud in front of an elder.

The oldest book in here draws Giza with a door in the side of it and a stair going down. Nobody has ever seen that door. Either the man who drew it had seen something, or he was a liar with a remarkably steady hand.

Somebody copied the Chichen calendar onto goatskin, in ink, wrong. Two of the marks are upside down. Every reader since has taken the upside down ones for the important ones, and that is what people mean when they say the stone speaks.

There are nine drawings of the Taj on that wall and not one of the Wall, and that tells more than the drawings do. Nobody draws the thing they are still arguing about. They draw the thing they have all finished agreeing on.
On a clear morning the Taj sits out there like something set down from a great height and not damaged. Everyone stops working. Even Neru stops, then says something rude about the roof to cover it.

They come over this pass in wet sandals on their way to the Wall, and I sell them soup, and I do not tell them there is no breach. Partly the soup money. Mostly because a person walking is a person not sitting down.

We build in steps here because Machu was built in steps, and ours slide every third spring, because they cut their stone to fit and we stack ours and hope. The same shape. Not remotely the same thing.

My grandson left to walk the Wall eleven years ago and sends word from further along every few winters. He has not found the breach. He has found a wife, two goats and a limp, which is a better return than most pilgrims manage.

Half this village reads the calendar and half loads the carts, and the readers are always the ones with less to carry. The stone at Chichen has said the same nothing for six generations and it will say it again next spring.

Somebody cut a little Petra into the seawall, doorways and all, about the size of a hand. It goes under at every high tide. They carved it knowing that. I would very much like to know who and not one person here will tell me.

They painted a pyramid on the boat shed for luck and got the sides too steep, so every pilgrim who passes stops to correct it, and Marek paints over the correction. Eleven times now. He would rather be right than dry.

Pilgrims come through on their way to walk the Wall. They ask which road and never ask what is under this street. A person hunting a breach two thousand miles off will step over a drowned door without once looking down.

Our terraces are copied off Machu badly, and the ledger says so in the ledger's own hand, which is the most honest thing anyone up here has ever written down. Then the same book gives careful instructions for building more of them.

Every winter the calendar reading gets copied into the record, and every winter it comes out as nonsense, and they file the nonsense beautifully. Three shelves of nothing, in order. I love them for it and I tell them so rarely.

There are two books on that shelf saying the Wall was never a dam at all, that it was a road along a ridge. The pilgrims are not shown those books. That was decided at a meeting, and I voted with the liars.

We measure the rise against a post here. The pilgrims measure it against Giza. The post says a hand a year. The pyramid says we are nine hands off the last mark. I bail regardless and let them do their arithmetic.

The old ones say that when the water touches the fourth course of stone at Giza it stops, because that is what the markers are there for. I have also rebuilt this raft three times. I believe both things before breakfast.
A raft is a terrace that gave up. Nobody says that on a hill, because the hill people take it badly and they are entirely right to. Down here we say it twice a day and mend the rope.

The dam broke in the north, that is what my father held to. Everybody's father held that it broke somewhere else. Nobody's father ever said the sea simply came, because that would mean nothing broke, and a thing that never broke cannot be mended.
Nobody left who remembers me young.
Teach the boy letters. He is slow either way.
I have outlived my own doorstep.
Ipa's name is cut in the beam. Say it sometimes.
Everyone climbs eventually. Some of us sit down first.
Thirty years mending that net. Not mending it now.
Plant the slow tree anyway.
My knees decide where I live now.
Sarn wanted the flat stone. Sarn got the flat stone.
Write it down or it goes with me.
Children learn nothing from a tidy story.
Nobody is coming. Good. Fewer mouths.
Ask me tomorrow. I will say the opposite.
Dorai's granddaughter is expecting. In this.
I taught four children. Three could spell my name.
There is no breach. They walk it anyway.
My mother's spoon is bent. Still a spoon.
Argue with me. Keeps my teeth sharp.
Somebody should learn the songs. Not me.
Old enough to be rude at last.
Renni thought the water would stop. Lovely woman. Wrong.
I stopped counting birthdays somewhere near eighty.
The ink fades before the paper goes.
Seeds in the third jar. Leave them.
Books keep better than people. Barely.
My mother is in the fourth alcove.
Good cold for the dead. Bad for me.
The lamp oil argument again. Every winter.
Copy the pages slowly. No hurry now.
Somebody has been sleeping in the seed room.
Deeper than the water can ever come. They say.
I know every name on that wall.
Thin soil. Thinner soup.
Nothing to bail up here. I miss it.
Wind takes the roof twice a winter.
Cannot see the sea. Smell it on visitors.
Higher is later, not never.
Fingers will not bend. So, talking.
We burn the chairs first.
Two goats. One is called Salt.
Stones enough here to bury everyone twice.
Half these doors stand open. Nobody is coming back.
The Mennas left the loom. The loom.
Deciding is the only work left on this street.
I go when the well turns. Not before.
Empty houses smell sweeter. Wrong, that.
They took the hinges and left the beds.
Two families this spring. Three last.
My whole street answers to nobody now.
Wait until I am dead. Then move.
The bell is still there. Nobody rings it.
We keep the ledger. It stops nothing.
Same measuring stick my father used.
Safe up here. I sleep worse.
The terraces are copied wrong. Walls too thin.
Put the names in the long book.
We left early. They have not forgotten.
Six marks on that post, a hand apart.
Our wells are sweet. That is the trouble.
Every child here reads. Every one.
Bail it. I am not dying dry.
This floor was a roof when I married.
My bed floats a little on spring tides.
Two buckets a day. My whole occupation.
Tie the ladder. I fell once.
The stilts outlived my husband. Cheap wood, too.
Do not repaint. Not this year.
Under this platform, not up that hill.
The Mennas moved up. Cowards. I miss them.
Sleep through the slap of it. Everyone does.
My sister Ipa is under nine feet of water and she still gets the first spoon at supper. Her name, anyway. We say it, then we eat. Two seconds, and it keeps the table honest.
They asked whether it is worth teaching the small ones their letters. I said no, to watch their faces. Then I taught them mine. Somebody has to spell the names on the stones after I stop.

Dorai's granddaughter is expecting, with the wells going brackish and the path washed out. I said nothing, which for me is remarkable. She wants to use her mother's name. That is reason enough for anything.
Everybody wants a last word. There is no last word. There is Tulu's roof, which leaks, and my hip, which also leaks, and market day, which comes regardless.
I have been wrong about the water four times. I said it would stop at the mill. Then at the shrine. Then at the second shrine. Now I do not say.
People want advice from an old man, so: mend the boat that gets used. I spent a whole winter on a hull I kept only for looking at.
When I go, put me where the goats can get at me. They are company, and they will eat the flowers, which saves somebody the weeding.
Half of them want to climb and half want to stay and drown politely. Let each be a fool in the direction they prefer. I have been both kinds. The food was better down here.
Four of us knew how to set a broken arm. Now there is me, and my hands shake. So I make Havi watch. He faints, but he faints later each time.
My brother Bakh said the water was a debt somebody owed. He also said he could hold his breath four minutes. He could not.
We moved twice. There will not be a third. My things know where they are and so do I, mostly.
I expect nothing. But the girl who fixed my chair did it better than I would have, with a joint nobody taught her. I will deny having said that.
I cannot remember my husband's voice at all. I remember that he chewed loudly and it drove me out of the room. The annoying parts are the sturdy ones.
The calendar stone gets read every spring by very serious people who then argue all the way down the path about what it said. It says nothing. I have looked. It is still a good day out.
They say the pointed markers were left by people who knew the water was coming. My mother said they were granaries. Either way they are still standing, which is more than the mill managed.

The seed jars are older than anyone's grandmother and every spring there is a fight about opening one. Last year they planted a handful of the barley just to see. It came up thin and sour and everybody wept, which was embarrassing for all concerned.

They burn good oil to copy books that nobody reads. I complained about it for thirty years. Then I learned my letters at sixty-one to check they were copying it right, and now I complain about the spelling.
My mother is in the fourth alcove, third along, wrapped in the good cloth because my sister insisted on it. I sit there and tell her about the neighbours. She was never a good listener alive either.
This cave has been slept in since before anybody was counting years. That is the one fact I find comforting, and I only find it comforting on dry days.
The children come in to trace the names on the wall with chalk dust on their fingers. They cannot read most of them. They do it anyway and then run out because it is cold, which is exactly right.

If anyone wonders whether any of it counts, look at the jars. Somebody a hundred years dead labelled them in a neat hand for a person they would never meet. Either idiotic, or the only sensible thing done here.
People climb here thinking height is an answer. Height is a delay with worse weather. I came up anyway, because my daughter is here and she cooks badly and requires supervision.
There is a boy up here who has never seen the sea. Not once. He asked whether it was loud. I said loud the way a very big room is loud, which is not an answer, but he wrote it down.
We put my wife under the flat rock where nothing grows, so nothing would grow on her. She hated flowers. She said flowers were showing off and she was not entirely joking.
The soup up here is water with an opinion. But nobody has changed house in forty years, so every child knows which room they were born in. Down at the water not one of them can tell you that.
Some of them want to go higher still, onto the bare shoulder where the wind takes a roof in one night. I said go, take the goats, and when you come back down do not explain.

In this cold my hands stopped working, so now I talk instead, which everyone regrets. I can still lay out my mother's kitchen. Door here, window there, jars along the north wall. Somebody should have that, even if it is only a goat listening.
Every house on this row belonged to somebody I could gossip about. Now I gossip with myself and I win every argument. Havi's mother is still here. She will not go while the fig fruits.
They keep asking when I will move. I say I am waiting for a sign. There is no sign. There is a well going salty and a daughter up the path, and one of those will win eventually.

I helped carry the Menna girl's chest up the path and then I walked back down. That is the whole thing. Everyone on this shore has hauled somebody else's furniture uphill and then gone home to a house that is going.
They keep asking whether moving matters. My cousin moved. He died in a dry bed complaining about the draught. I will die in a wet one complaining about the damp. He was not happier.
The school room lost its shutters but the slate wall is still standing. Two of us take turns with whoever is left. Four children some days, one the next. We teach the same letters over. Nobody minds.

The trick is to leave before you have to, which nobody does, myself included. I have watched three families pack in a single night with the water at the step. Undignified. I intend to do exactly the same.

They keep everything in the long book up here. Whose grandmother, which house, which year it went. I looked up mine. It says: Vasi, dwelling below the mill, lost. Four words for a kitchen with a blue floor.
The hill people came up before the rest and have been apologising for eighty years by writing things down. Fine. Somebody should. But not one of them can gut a fish without making a mess of it.
I moved up when my knees went and I have not been properly warm since. But the children here read, all of them, even the difficult one. That is what the cold bought.

They copy the terraces from the old stone place across the water and get it wrong every time. Walls too thin, drains in the wrong corner. Still standing, though. Wrong and standing is most of what people are.
The record keeper asked me for every name in my mother's house. I got to eleven and stopped. Not because I was upset. Because I could not remember the cousin with the ears.
I told them to stop writing down water numbers and start writing down how the fish stew is made. They wrote both, of course, in two neat columns. Insufferable people. They were right.
Our floor is the ceiling of the room I was born in. On slack water you can see the blue plaster through the boards. My mother mixed that blue. She would be furious that we walk on it.
They came down from the hill to tell me it is time to move. Fourth time. I gave them tea, let them talk, then went out to bail. That was my answer and they understood it.
We do letters on the raft when the wind is low. The chalk runs, the boards swell, half of it washes off by evening. They still know their letters, which surprises everybody including me.
A person bails every day of their life and then one day they do not, and that is the whole story of this village. I have made peace with the bucket. It is a good bucket.
When Sarn died the ground was long gone, so we weighted him and put him under the platform. I knock on the boards before I sleep. It is not a prayer. It is knocking.

Everything here has been temporary for sixty years. Temporary is a fine way to live. And the knots these young ones tie are better than the ones my father tied, which is either progress or an insult to my father.

lore.text: Lamp soot has built into a stripe along the passage roof, thickest where a person of average height has to duck.
Water drips into a stone basin at a rate that fills it by morning. The basin is worn into a bowl deeper than a head.
The air in here is the temperature the outside was four months ago.
Ochre handprints run along the low passage at the height of a walking adult, and one line of them at the height of a child.
Seed jars sit in rows in the cold chamber, labelled by hand, and partway along the row the labels stop being paper and start being bark.
The floor of the entrance hall has been swept for so many lifetimes that it now sits a finger lower than the doorstep.
The dead lie in the fourth chamber with their feet toward the entrance. The oldest lie the other way about, and the turning happened inside a single generation.
A comb, a fishing weight and a milk tooth share one niche in the wall. Nothing labels them. Nothing needs to.
Books are stacked spine out in the dry chamber. The ones about the sea have been read to pieces. The ones about horses are perfect.
Somebody has copied a whole book by hand into the margins of another book, having run out of everything except ink.
Grain jars line the wall in two sizes. The larger size stopped being made about sixty years back, and every survivor of it is patched with pitch.
Seven shapes are painted in a row on the deep chamber wall: a triangle, a long line, a ring, a stair, a comb, a doorway, a dome. The dome is repainted most often.
A charcoal drawing of a ring of arches has a water line ruled across it, and under it somebody much younger has drawn lions with very long necks.
A calendar of small squares is cut into the rock by the entrance. The squares run out four hundred years ago and the counting continues on the wall beside them in a different hand.
The seed jars have been sorted into two sets. One is sealed with wax and stands at the back. The other is opened every spring.
The newest thing in here is a shelf, planed smooth and pegged, empty, built to the size of books that have not been written.
Silt lies flat over the floor tiles, undisturbed except where a fish has fanned it into a comma.
A shutter still swings on one hinge, slow, timed to a swell that arrives every eleven seconds.
Weed grows only on the south walls. The rest is bare stone, scrubbed pale by the water that runs through the doorway all day and half the night.
The lane runs straight between the roofs for forty strokes, then stops at a step that goes up into nothing.
A well stands in the middle of the square. The bucket is still knotted to its rope, hanging in water, above water.
Three storeys of shelving in what was a shop. The top shelf is bare. Everything below it is still stacked, and still in order.
A child's height marks are cut into a doorframe, five of them, the highest at chest level. Barnacles have taken the lowest two.
Someone has tied a red cord around the handle of the third door on the left. The knot is new. The door has not been opened.
In the corner room a table is laid for four. Three of the plates are gone. The fourth sits under a finger of sand with the spoon still crossed over it.
A cooking pot hangs above a hearth full of clean sand. Nobody took it. It was too heavy, or it was hers.
Notches climb the lintel of the widest doorway, a hand's width apart, and a newer one has been scratched above the rest at a careless angle.
Cord loops hang from the sunken gatepost, one for each visit made. The oldest have gone to green fur and lost their knots.
The temple floor is a spiral of small tiles. Two turns from the centre a repair has been made in the wrong colour, and the wrong colour is itself very old.
Flowers weighted with a stone sit on the sill of an upper window. They are not yet limp. Someone swam down this week.
In the schoolroom the benches are stacked against the wall the way benches are stacked at the end of a term. No one came back to put them down.
A rope ladder is lashed to the balcony rail. New hemp, tight turns, tied by somebody who meant to come back down it and did.
Snowmelt runs to the door in a split log and freezes overnight in the same crook of the wood every time.
Wool is stretched on frames outside each house, stiff with cold, still smelling of the animal it came off.
The hearths burn dung and moss. More smoke than heat, and the smoke has cured the roof beams black and sweet.
There is no path down the far side. There was a village at the bottom of it once, so there was a path once.
Weather comes up the valley off the water now instead of over the ridge, and every door in the row was built on the wrong side.
The cairns on the ridge stand a day's walk apart. The lowest three are gone.
A boat's nameboard is nailed above a door up here where no boat has any business, salt bleached, carried the whole way by somebody's grandfather.
In the hut by the pass a jar of sea salt sits on the shelf, unopened, older than anyone who has slept in the room.
The burial ground is scree. The dead go under stacked stones, and the stack for a child is not smaller, it is only neater.
One household keeps a pair of oars. There is no water within four days in any direction. The oars are oiled.
A drawing scratched on the rock face shows a wall running along a ridge, longer than the ridge is, with a gap in it. The gap has been rubbed out and redrawn twice.
Walkers stop here for the night before going north. Each leaves one stone on the pile by the door and takes nothing away.
The stone table by the pass is scored with lines and a ring of marks that people still count on their fingers, arriving at different answers, arguing warmly.
The year is counted here in lambs. There is no ledger, and nobody has yet felt the want of one.
Two empty houses stand with their doors wedged open, floors swept, firewood stacked, in the manner of a place expecting company.
Children born up here have never seen the sea. They draw it as a grey field, flat, with one hut standing in the middle of it.
The swell out here comes long and low, and the boat rises to it without a sound from the timbers.
A raft of weed drifts past with small crabs riding in it, going somewhere at the speed of the current.
Birds are working a patch of water half a morning east. They do not stay long over any one place.
The water changes colour along a straight edge and holds that line as far as the eye can follow it.
The lead line goes down and down and at last touches on something flat.
The bottom shoals abruptly and the shallow runs off in a straight line for a long way, the way only a made thing runs.
A stone spire breaks the surface far from any land, birds nesting in its top window, and nothing else of it shows at all.
Fish school here around a shape below that is too regular to be rock. The spot is known by a family name and not by a landmark.
Floats mark out a rectangle of open water with nothing in it worth catching. The corners are exactly square.
Cold fresh water rises here in a plume a swimmer feels on the back of the leg. There was a spring, and the spring has not stopped.
On a clear day something down there throws back a green light, at a depth the eye keeps guessing wrong.
Along this stretch every boat drops a stone over the side without breaking its rowing, and nobody explains it to the young until they ask.
A pole has been driven into the bottom out here and stands three arms clear of the surface, painted in bands, the lowest bands eaten away to bare wood.
The sailing lines run to a notch in the mountain and a stone tooth on the far horizon. They are kept in songs, and the songs are older than the boats.
This stretch is thick with fish and nobody works it. The reason has softened over the years into a habit that nobody minds keeping.
Cut wood drifts by, sawn square and pegged, four boards still fixed together, going out with the current and not in.
Salt has bloomed white on the lower courses of every wall, waist high, and stops there in a clean line.
Four houses along this row still have doors. Two have doorways. Nobody has taken the hinges yet.
A dog sleeps in the warmest part of the road, which is the part with no roof left over it.
Chalk numbers on the gable ends: how many winters each house has left, guessed by somebody with a steady hand.
The upper street is lived in. The street below it is where they keep goats. The street below that is where they keep nothing.
Fig trees in the low gardens have died back from the leaves down, and the roots showing through the soil have gone the colour of old rope.
Furniture stands in the square under sailcloth, chalked with family marks, waiting on a decision that was due last spring.
One house has been half taken apart for its beams and then left. The walls are down to the sills. The roof is untouched.
The graveyard has been laid out again a field higher, the same stones in the same arrangement, and there is nothing under most of them.
The bread oven in the middle of the row is hot. It serves nine households, four of which went up the hill years ago and still come down for it.
Three stone terraces have been started on the slope above the town, each shorter than the last, copied from something remembered rather than seen.
The shrine on the point holds a smooth carved stone that belongs to nobody's god, kept because it is older than the water and nothing else here is.
A stepped tower of dry stone stands at the field edge, waist high, flat on top, with nothing on it. Children rebuild it whenever a goat knocks it down.
Two carts stand loaded and roped in the yard, and have stood so since the weather turned. The oxen are out grazing.
In the last full house a wall of names and heights and dates has been copied onto a board small enough for one person to carry.
The well has a new lid, dovetailed and hinged and planed smooth. Somebody spent a week of good weather on it.
Beans climb strings on the third terrace. The wall behind them holds the day's heat until well after dark.
Every roof is weighted with grey stones laid in the same overlapping order, because the wind here comes from one direction and never learns another.
A stone channel runs the length of the lane, dry, with a wooden plug lying beside it ready for rain.
The terrace walls are cut blocks that do not match the local rock. They were carried up. The sledge ruts are still in the path.
From the lookout bench the whole valley is water with three roofs standing in it. The bench faces that way on purpose.
The oldest terrace here is the highest one and the newest is the lowest, which is the opposite of the way a village usually grows.
The record house keeps ledgers of who came up in which year. The later years are written in a hand that presses harder.
A shelf of house keys hangs in the record house, tagged and ordered, for doors that are now under eleven arms of water.
Each section of terrace wall carries the name of the family that built it. Two sections carry no name, and the stonework there is just as good.
A room is kept for people arriving. The bedding is aired every month. It has been slept in four times in nine years.
Every terrace is cut to the same width, and the width is wrong for the slope, and everyone knows it, and nobody will be the first to change it.
In the record house a drawing of a stepped mountain city hangs where the light will not reach it, redrawn each generation from the drawing before.
The field walls are laid without mortar, stone shaved to fit stone, in imitation of a place nobody in this village has ever walked.
The school teaches reading, which the waterline villages let go of. The results are two shelves of books and one child who has read both.
Grain is stored well past what the ledger calls need. The number in the margin is the number of people down the hill, counted twice.
A new stair has been cut into the cliff going down toward the water, wide enough for two abreast, with a handrail. Nobody up here says who it is for.
Every plank on the walkway is a different age. The newest is pale and springs underfoot.
Bailing tins hang by each door, handles worn smooth, one for every person in the hut including the small ones.
Split fish dry under the eaves with their tails all pointing the same way, out of habit rather than wind.
The stilts are scarred with paint bands where the deck used to sit. Three bands, three raisings, the lowest one under weed.
A ladder leans from the pontoon into the water and keeps going. Four rungs are still used. The rest belong to the fish.
Under the boards a second village of barnacles has taken the old handrails, which stand down there straight and useless.
A raft is roped alongside with a woman's name burned into the transom and a patch of newer wood driven right through the middle of it.
Inside the net hut, tide heights are scratched into the plank year by year, and one year is circled hard enough to cut the wood.
A chimney breaks the surface twenty strokes out. Children use it as the turning post. The family that built it still lives in sight of it.
A cradle is lashed to the roof beam, up out of the wet, still lashed there though the girl who slept in it has grey in her plait.
Small stone squares with stepped sides sit in a row along the pontoon rail, cut by hand, every one of them facing the far mountain.
A shutter is painted with water and a line ruled across it, and the line is above the water, and the shutter is repainted every spring.
The rope work here copies a pattern that runs along the old wall to the north. The knot is wrong. Everybody ties it wrong in exactly the same way.
The school raft has benches for eleven and nine children. The two spare are kept clear, which is not the same as expecting anyone.
Fresh timber has been floated in and stacked. Enough to lift the walkway again, or enough for one large boat. Nobody has cut it yet.
A grandmother's chair is bolted to the deck facing the water. It has been unbolted and set higher twice, and the old holes are plugged with wax.
Iguanas hold the top step as though they pay for it. By midmorning the stone is too hot to stand on barefoot and the shade on the north side is crowded.
Clap once at the foot of the stair and the stone claps back, higher, like a bird. Children do it until an adult stops them.
Green water stands in the sinkhole behind the pyramid and is not going down. Cut steps lead toward it and end below the surface.
The lowest three tiers wear a skirt of weed. Small fish work the corners where the mortar has gone soft and sweet.
The ninth step is worn into a shallow dish at its left end. Somebody sat there a great many mornings, always in the same place, always facing the same way.
A slate lies face down under a stone at the foot of the stair. Damp has taken half the tally. The last row is still crossed off in fives, up to sixty-eight.
Chalk stubs, a folded blanket and an empty gourd sit in the shade of the north stair. The blanket is dry. Whoever brought it out means to come back.
Four hands have counted the steps in charcoal along one balustrade. Three totals agree and one does not, and the odd one has been circled twice, hard enough to score the stone.
Late in the day a line of shadow steps down the north edge joint by joint. Pegs have been driven into the ground where its point falls. The pegs are numbered and the numbers do not run in order.
A carved panel is rubbed pale where hands read it, always at the same three figures. The rest stays crusted with lichen. Nobody has touched the part showing people carrying water.
A whole season of tallies has been scraped off the balustrade and the stone left bare. Underneath, an older tally shows through, uncounted, in a hand nobody living writes like.
One mark at the top of the stair was made this morning, beside a knot of cord holding the running count. The cord is very long. Whoever ties it has not skipped a day in years.
Gulls own the upper arches and argue about it constantly. Fig trees have got into the seams and are winning.
Wind through the arches makes one low note that changes when the wind turns. People nearby use it instead of looking up.
The bowl is full. Water stands flat inside the ring and slaps the inner wall on the seaward side, where the stone has come away in slabs.
Children swim the flooded floor. A stub of fallen column is the thing you touch before you are allowed to turn back.
A knotted rope hangs from an arch into the water and the stone above it is worn shiny by hands. Two names are cut there, one much deeper than the other.
A stair goes down into the green and keeps going. On the third step under the surface a clay pot stands upright, still where it was set down.
Onions are growing in a basket of soil on the second tier, lashed in place with net cord. That soil came up the stair one handful at a time.
The lower wall carries hundreds of chalk lions, nearly all of them at child height. Every one has a long tongue reaching down to the water.
A rough wooden lion stands in a niche, its nose worn pale from being touched. It has too many teeth and its legs are all different lengths.
Buckets are stacked by the seaward arch and more hang on pegs above them. The rims are white with salt crust and not one of them looks recently used.
A tin ladle hangs on a nail at the waterline with a strip of cloth tied through its handle. Somebody still dips it, tastes, and hangs it back. The nail is worn bright.
New chalk on the inner wall shows a lion with a line struck through it, then the same lion drawn again beside it without the line. Both hands look about the same age.
The stone holds yesterday's heat well past dark. Lizards come out for it, flat against the south face, and do not move when a shadow crosses them.
Wind has polished the lower courses smooth enough to see a face in. Higher up the blocks are still rough and still furred with old mortar.
A dark band runs along the third course, level the whole way around, wider than a hand. Above it the stone is pale as a picked bone.
Two boats are tied to an iron ring driven into the stone. The ring is old and weeping rust. The knots are not old at all.

Someone has cut a shallow notch into the fourth course and scratched a name beside it. Below it are six more notches and six more names, the lowest one underwater now and still legible through the green.
A rope ladder hangs down the north face, its bottom rungs furred with weed. Whoever uses it keeps the top three dry and replaces them often.
A tin cup sits wedged in a joint near the waterline, half full of rain. Beside it, a small handprint in tar, set at exactly arm's reach from the ladder.
High on the east face, well above any water, one notch has been cut and squared and cut again. Every other mark on this thing sits below it. Somebody wanted that to mean something.
Charcoal lines cover a single block, dozens of them, each with a number under it. They disagree by whole courses. Two have been scrubbed at and written over in a different hand.
Fresh chips of limestone lie heaped at the base where the old marks are being deepened. The tool is still there, a bent spike with cloth wound round the grip, left where it can be found again.
A new notch sits a hand above the deepest, squarest cut on the east face. It is raw and white, and nobody has scratched a name beside it yet.
The rope ladder has been lengthened twice, once with rope and once with knotted net. Somebody still climbs it early, and the wet handprints are gone off the stone by noon.
Grass grows in the joints along the top and lies flat where the feet go. The wind across the ridge is hard enough to lean on.
A tower roof has fallen in and filled the room below with clean broken tile. Swallows use the one beam left standing.
The wall comes down the ridge, crosses the flat and goes into the water without pausing. On a clear day its line is visible under the surface a long way out.
At the low end the parapet is barnacled to chest height. The gaps in it make a row of small pools that never quite drain.
The path along the top is worn to a pale stripe down the middle of the stone, ankle deep in places. Nobody has walked the edges in a very long time.
A pair of sandals sits neatly beside a tower door, soles worn through at the ball of the foot, laces still tied. Whoever left them went on barefoot.
Somebody has been living in the third tower: a straw bed, a hook for a pot, and firewood cut short to fit round the stair.
Every tower has a number chalked inside the doorway and most have three or four, in different hands, disagreeing. Under one of them the same word is written four times, each time smaller.
Cairns stand along the parapet, one every few hundred paces, each stone laid by a different hand. Walkers add one and keep going. The cairns run down to the water and do not stop there.
A strip of cloth is tied to the parapet at a place where the stone is sound and unbroken. The knot has been retied many times. Somebody keeps coming back to this exact spot.
Charcoal on a tower wall lists towers by number with a stroke through each, hundreds of strokes, the writing getting smaller and steadier toward the end. There is no note at the bottom.
A family has taken the seventh tower and hung a door on it. Their children run the worn stripe of the path back and forth, going nowhere in particular, shouting.
Mist sits in the terraces until midmorning and then leaves the ridge all at once. Everything drips for an hour afterward.
The joints take no blade and hold no moss. Grass grows right up to the stone and stops there.
Rain runs the cut channels the whole length of the place and comes out clean at the bottom, still running, still going exactly where it was sent.
From the top terrace the valley is a flat sheet of water with roof ridges standing in it, and the pale line of a road going down under.
Four knotted measuring cords hang from a peg by the stair, each a different length, each with its knots spaced differently.
A straight stick has been laid against one wall joint and traced along in charcoal, over and over. The charcoal line never quite matches the stone.
A hide is pegged out flat in the lee of a wall with a wall drawn on it, stone by stone. One corner of the drawing has been scratched out and started again.
A short length of wall stands apart from the rest, newly built, its stones fat and hand-shaped and thickly mortared. The mortar has cracked already. It has been repointed twice.
Dust and chips have gathered at the base of an old wall where visitors pick at one joint to find how deep it goes. The joint goes deeper than the picking.
Pegs and cord mark out terrace corners, the spacing copied outward from a middle point. The copy drifts. By the tenth terrace it is a full pace wrong.
On the slope below, a young terrace is planted and holding: beans, a brush windbreak, a drain cut in the wrong place but cut anyway. Its wall bulges and has been shored with a log.
Tools lie by the far wall, worn into different shapes by different hands. The newest handle is bound with fresh cord. Somebody has been learning here a long time and is not finished.
The gorge runs narrow and red and the wind in it never entirely stops. Sound arrives well before the person does.
Channels cut at shoulder height run the whole length of the passage, dry now, drifted with sand and goat pellets.
Rain comes down the gorge in one push and leaves a fresh line of grit along the walls. The line sits higher each year and nobody sweeps it.
At the seaward end of the valley the water stands, and the carved fronts there are knee deep in their own reflection.
A camp sits in the shade of the tallest facade: three cook fires, none of them new, and a windbreak of stacked stone added to by several different builders.
A folding stool has been left facing the carved front with a blanket still over it. The blanket is worn through in the two places where elbows go.
Small chisel scars sit low on the doorframe, in a spot where nothing needed carving. The powder from them is still white on the sand.
Two columns of scratched marks run down either side of the entrance, tallying some argument. One column is far longer. The shorter one is being added to at night in a childish hand.
A hollow has been cut into the facade to show the rock behind it, then abandoned partway. Whatever that was meant to settle, the person cutting it stopped.
Sea shells are pressed into a mortar patch beside the door in neat rows, far higher than any water has ever come. Somebody put them there on purpose and left no word about it.
Children keep their own tally on a boulder outside the gorge, copied badly, both columns kept even. They cross one off each side at the same moment so that neither can win.
One patch of sand by the facade is pressed smooth in the shape of a stool that is no longer there. The tally beside the door has not grown in a while and rain has softened the newest marks.
The white stone throws light back so hard that the shade under the arch reads as black. Parakeets go in and out of a broken vent above the door.
Feet are quiet here. The floor is smooth enough that people walk it flat and slow without anyone telling them to.
The long pool has joined the sea. The reflection sits unbroken except where a fish takes something off the surface.
The lowest step is under water and gone green, and the one above it is wet twice a day. People stop at the third step without discussing it.
Offerings crowd the ledge inside the door: shells, a bone comb with two teeth gone, a knot of hair set in wax, a child's tooth on a scrap of cloth.
Names are cut into the plinth in small close letters, round the corner and along the side. New ones go into whatever gaps are left.
A rope of dried flowers hangs from a nail beside the arch. Beneath it the marble carries a dark patch where a hundred ropes hung before.
The inlaid stone at hand height has been rubbed until the pattern is only a shine. Higher up, the same flowers keep their red and their green.
Nothing here is scratched out. Every other wall in this world carries some argument crossed through by somebody, and this one carries only names.
Two lamps burn in the chamber, filled by different people at different hours, one with fish oil and one with something sweeter. Neither has been allowed to go out.
The chamber floor was swept this morning and the sweepings left piled by the door: petals, sand, a fish scale, a single blue bead. Nobody has thrown the pile away.
Somebody came a long way for this. A boat lies on the mud below with its sail still rigged and its fire gone cold, and on the step above the water, sandals set neatly side by side.
